source.title: Transcoder Adapters for Reasoning-Model Diffing
source.authors: Nathan Hu; Jake Ward; Thomas Icard; Christopher Potts

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether descriptions of neuron-activating examples predict activation on new text, using an automated detection measure rather than auditing the share of neuron poles with one or two jobs.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an automated detection score for MLP neurons. Its other feature-classification results concern adapter features or classify neurons by reasoning/domain/language category; they do not measure the share of neuron poles with one main job. The paper does not audit Qwen3-32B poles, compare model scales or architectures, or test the essay’s InceptionV1 claims.
record.test_reason: The paper's main aim is model diffing with transcoder adapters. As baselines it reports two results on MLP neurons of 7B dense models: (1) a Bills-style automated detection score for neuron descriptions on new text, and (2) an LLM-judge classification of neurons from activating examples, including an 'uninterpretable' share. Both bear on how well neurons are explained by their activating examples (V6) and on the not-understood share in another dense LM (V2), using methods different from the essay's pole audit.
record.authors_conclusion: Roughly right. The authors conclude that adapter features are sparse and interpretable, scoring slightly higher in automated detection than MLP neurons (0.82–0.84 vs 0.80). Neuron class frequencies barely differ between base and reasoning models, suggesting reasoning fine-tuning changes overall computation little. Only a small fraction of adapter features look reasoning-specific. Hesitation is governed by about 5.6k simple features.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses the automated feature-description and detection pipeline associated with Bills et al. to compare transcoder-adapter features with MLP neurons; it does not perform the original Qwen3 pole audit.
record.method_sensitivity: For adapter features, detection scores differ with example sampling: max-activating examples score 0.82–0.84, while uniformly sampled activating examples score 0.69–0.73. The reported neuron score uses max-activating examples.

fits_no_version.finding: For transcoder-adapter features (not neurons), detection accuracy drops from 0.82–0.84 with max-activating examples to 0.69–0.73 with uniformly sampled activating examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanations derived from top activations overstate predictive accuracy across a feature's full activation range (dictionary features rather than neurons).

record.problems: For the neuron result, the paper does not specify which model’s neurons underlie the 0.80 score, give uncertainty estimates, report per-neuron scores, or define a threshold for a good score.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results meet the row criteria for the claim versions: the feature-class frequency results classify reasoning/domain/language categories rather than one-main-job poles, and other outcomes concern adapter behavior or model diffing.

missing.what: LLM-judge classification of MLP neurons. Qwen2.5-Math-7B neurons: 60.8% language, 29.9% domain, 3.3% reasoning, 6.1% uninterpretable. record.verdict_notes: The neuron results are side baselines in a model-diffing paper, not a dedicated audit. The judge prompt frames neurons as SAE features and anchors on '10-30% uninterpretable', which may bias the shares. Which model's neurons gave the 0.80 detection score is unstated. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole audit and its one-job, two-related-jobs, and not-understood shares.
Shares across other language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or trillion-parameter scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, shared pose features, and recursive generalization.
Architecture/tool effects on interpretable-neuron shares and the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
The paper tests prediction on new text with an automated detection pipeline, but does not directly establish how much of each neuron’s function is explained or assess one-main-job pole labels.
The paper reports a neuron detection score but not the fraction of neurons above a stated threshold for a good score; it does not test stronger explainer models.

rows.subject: MLP neurons (model not specified)
rows.operation_detail: Generated descriptions from max-activating examples and tested whether they predict activation on new text snippets.
rows.note: The paper reports this score for MLP neurons without specifying which model’s neurons or giving a distribution across individual neurons. The score is imperfect, but it does not reveal what fraction of neurons meet a threshold for a good score.
rows.check: Subject should be MLP neurons of the 7B Qwen2.5-Math / R1-Distill-Qwen models; the paper does not say which, and the R1-Distill target is likely. Positives in the detection test are activating examples, apparently max-activating for neurons, and negatives are random snippets. A 0.80 mean (chance 0.50) shows explanations miss about 20% of judgments, a partial version of V6's failure. It bears on V7 only weakly: this is binary detection, not activation simulation, and no per-neuron distribution or 'good score' share is given. So V7 cannot be determined from this row.

source_check.problem: Model for the 0.80 neuron score is not stated; row correctly says so. Negatives are random Open Thoughts texts, not matched non-activating neuron examples.

relationships.condition: MLP neurons of a 7B Qwen2.5-based model; GPT-4o-mini explainer and detector; max-activating examples
relationships.reason: Descriptions written from activating examples predict activation on new snippets at only 0.80 accuracy (chance 0.50), so about a fifth of judgments fail (r1). Evidence is weak: the test uses max-activating positives and gives no per-neuron breakdown.
relationships.display_finding: Descriptions written from activating examples predicted activation on new snippets at only 0.80 accuracy against 0.50 chance, so about a fifth of judgments failed. The evidence is weak because the test uses max-activating positives and gives no per-neuron breakdown.

source_check.notes: Fig. 7's text is garbled. The model-to-column mapping still checks out: the columns sum to 100% (60.8+29.9+3.3+6.1; 59.2+31.8+3.1+5.9), and the text notes more domain neurons in the reasoning model. The 0.80 neuron detection score names no model and gives no distribution or uncertainty. The number of neurons classified for Fig. 7 is not stated.

statements.correction: The uninterpretable shares come from a GPT-5-mini judge classification (Section 5.2, Fig. 7, Appendix E): up to 10 max-activating examples plus top logits; categories language/domain/reasoning/uninterpretable. The Bills-style detection pipeline (Appendix F, GPT-4o-mini) gives only the 0.80 neuron detection score. Fig. 7 does not state how many neurons were classified. The judge prompt was written for SAE features and cites a rough 10-30% uninterpretable guide.
statements.problem: Numbers are right: 6.1% (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) and 5.9% (R1-Distill) uninterpretable; 60.8/29.9/3.3 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. But the conditions line lists the Bills-style detection pipeline, which does not produce these shares. That pipeline uses GPT-4o-mini and gives only the 0.80 neuron detection score.
